dated_statements.statement: This is October 10th [2017], and we're on the 1000 line [Road].
dated_statements.speaker: Bob Zybach

dated_statements.statement: Well this was all privately owned land, where we are, until the 1920s.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: When we came in here in 1955, when the Elliott forest became under management by the State Department of Forestry, we decided that bridges are difficult and expensive to maintain, so we tried to relocate this road in many places so it wouldn't have bridges.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: 1958, something like that?
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: So they may have burned about 1750 or 1770, but nothing since then?
dated_statements.speaker: Bob Zybach

dated_statements.statement: The fire of 1868 hit the young Weyerhaeuser timber, and went out.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: So the ridge line up there is the boundary of the 1868 fire?
dated_statements.speaker: Bob Zybach

dated_statements.statement: So, when you say old growth, you mean trees that lasted through the 1800's fire.
dated_statements.speaker: Amber Ross

dated_statements.statement: The 1750 or 1770 fire?
dated_statements.speaker: Bob Zybach

dated_statements.statement: When that fire in 1868 burned, they were too young to be commercial.
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: When you're saying old growth on the trees that escaped the 1868 fire, are you saying like 200 year old trees or how old?
dated_statements.speaker: Bob Zybach

dated_statements.statement: No, in 1868 they would've been .
dated_statements.speaker: Jerry Phillips

dated_statements.statement: The trees that were old growth, that you're referring to as old growth, were those trees that were like 200 years old ones that survived the 1868 fire?
dated_statements.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.text: Tape 1-B. Interview with Jerry Phillips by Bob Zybach with Amber Ross and Randy Wiest while touring the Elliott State Forest on October 10, 2017. Part 1. Allegany to the Elliott on Marlow Creek [1000] Road

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. This is October 10th [2017], and we're on the 1000 line [Road]. Jerry Phillips, Randy Wiest, Amber Ross, me, Bob Zybach, and we're making an oral history recording and we've all agreed that these words can be used on the Internet and so on. Let's see, Jerry, Randy, do you have anything to say?

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: I do not.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, Amber?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: No.
Stop #A-01. 0:50 Buehner’s Logging Camp. Photos (4): 0864; 0865; 0866; 0867

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. Jerry, we're on the 1000 Road, it used to be a railroad grade, and we're by the old logging camp. Can you say the history of this road, kind of tell us what happened here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well this was all privately owned land, where we are, until the 1920s. I met the man who had worked for the Buehner & Stout Logging Company. They were the ones who built the railroad. And his job was to go out ahead, up the canyon here, and to decide which land they should buy for logging.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This railroad had 7 bridges across Marlow Creek, and includes inclines up some of the steep ridge ground, to harvest there. The logs were all moved out of here by railroad and splashed in the Millacoma River, down by Allegany, down to their mill in the Coos Bay-North Bend area. When we came in here in 1955, when the Elliott forest became under management by the State Department of Forestry, we decided that bridges are difficult and expensive to maintain, so we tried to relocate this road in many places so it wouldn't have bridges.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Was it still a railroad grade at that time or were they using it for automobiles?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It had been abandoned. I'm going to guess in the mid '40s, it was abandoned for use. And the fire patrol, Coos Fire Patrol, tried to maintain it for a while because it was considered a high hazard area for fire possibility. So they just kept it marginally open for that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What was the reason for the fire? Was it old buildings and logging debris?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's because of the old logging debris from the railroad days. So there were a lot of snags and unburned slash in here that was a possible fire area.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So when you opened this up in '55 for logging and you're realigning the railroad, was there still any of the old railroad shacks or any of the logging equipment or anything here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Just upstream of where we are now, maybe another two miles up from here, there was a blacksmith shop.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's where we want to stop next.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Because of course the railroad itself had engines and log cars, so that called for a lot of maintenance, including blacksmith work. It became kind of a land mark, where someone was above or below the blacksmith shop.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well this spur right here, where did this go?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: This spur took the place of an old incline where it was too steep for a road, and besides what they were doing was railroad logging, so they would put an incline up some area. It was just a little bit upstream from here. And with a donkey up on top, they'd lower these loaded cars down to the bottom, where the railroad mainline was.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: So we converted this into a road. It was a long corner of old-growth, mostly red cedar, clear up at the end of this two-mile road to the left, and in those days it was considered you could spend $10 a thousand [board feet, or MBF] on building an access road. That was a kind of Board [of Forestry] imposed limit. So that gave us $20,000 to build this two miles of road. And since it was all dirt it was possible. There was no rock to be blown in building this right here. Our engineer was brand new, George Shore, it was part of his original job was to lay out this two miles of dirt road to reach that long corner of old-growth.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: If I wanted to take a photo that approximates the photo of the logging camp, would it be from this location?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I'd say just probably a hundred feet up here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay. And then this incline here, this was built to go back to old- growth cedar?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The incline was a little further upstream. So this is where our engineer decided to put the road, so this would be all dirt here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But where did this road go?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It goes up onto South Marlow Ridge, that's the name we gave it, South Marlow Ridge Road. It goes and it dead-ends maybe four miles up here on the ridge top.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Is there any reason to drive this road?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I don't think so.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, it just goes up to an old cedar . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well to a number of old harvest areas. We did quite a bit of harvesting on this road. A lot of hardwoods, a lot of it red alder. Some hemlock. Not fir because that was all harvested in the railroad days. So all you'd see is young fir and alder up the ridge.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So the alder followed the original logging, it wasn't an understory or anything.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yes, that's right. And as you can see, as we go up this road, all this alder and maple is from that railroad logging days.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But when the railroad logged it was old-growth Doug fir?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was. Well, fir and cedar, of course red cedar. And then some hemlock. Now I don't know if they actually hauled the hemlock out or not. Hemlock's been considered to be a very, very low value species, so they might not have hauled it out.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So let's say about where that elderberry is, about where the photo would be?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Where the patch of alder is right here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay, I'm not gonna wade through the blackberry. I'll take a picture of it, of the location.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah. The picture was taken back this way.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, I'm gonna take a quick picture, I can leave that [recorder] running.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Today this is considered part of a fishery stream. The biologists really like it. It has three or four species of fish that they use. I think steelhead and coho and of course trout.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: How do you pronounce the name of the town that was here, or the logging site?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was Buehner & Stout Logging Company.

entries.text: Oh, what was the original name? Was it just called the railroad grade or when you made it into a road what did you called it?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Just Marlow Creek road.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Marlow Creek road?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative).

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They got a number assigned later on, but that was originally just called Marlow Creek Road.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay, and then it became the 1000.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative). And one of the reasons it became a main road is because the land is commingled up here between Weyerhaeuser and the State. And Weyerhaeuser's done a lot of logging. One of the first things we did here was enter into a mutual agreement with Weyerhaeuser, so that they would pay for their share of the maintenance every year. So we got to be able to calculate how much volume we hauled over the road and how much that Weyerhaeuser hauled over the road, and then they would pay their proportionate percentage.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We simply used their contribution . . . Not really contribution, but their share, for maintenance. Including the lower end down here where we were on pavement there for a while. We used their share to cover some of the maintenance. It worked out very well.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Is there anything between the old logging camp here and the blacksmith shop that you can think of to stop or look at or consider?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, we'll come to Y Creek, and that is where the incline came down the hill.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Nothing else I can think of.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay, let's see.

entries.text: This was a Christmas tree plantation?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No. Not a plantation. Just how it grew back.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: After the original logging, how it grew back. And then that was all logged a few years ago, and then that's gonna be it. That's the third stand on it. All Weyerhaeuser.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I'm sure there's been a hundred million feet all on this road here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: All old growth?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah old growth. Almost all.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: So, when you say old growth, you mean trees that lasted through the 1800's fire. Regenerated after that?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Ones that were . . .Yeah pretty much that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The 1750 or 1770 fire?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: When that fire in 1868 burned, they were too young to be commercial.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: They would've been 90 or 100 years old then?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They were ones that the fire didn't want to burn. Fires like to burn second growth. Course here you call it third growth, in Coos County. But the fire only took lengths. On a south slope with some wind, it'll climb over anything. It'll burn solid maple. A fire burn on an ordinary flat or gentle ground, it doesn't want to burn the new growth. So this whole area is Weyerhaeuser tree farm, we're still inside the Weyerhaeuser tree farm.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: When you're saying old growth on the trees that escaped the 1868 fire, are you saying like 200 year old trees or how old?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No, in 1868 they would've been . . . to the left.

entries.speaker: Randy Wiest
entries.text: Left?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Weyerhaeuser spur there. Everything you see here is Weyerhaeuser. And it was all logged after the Columbus Day windstorm because it had all blown down and it all grew up again and it was also harvested again. So this is the third stand for this.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: The trees that were old growth, that you're referring to as old growth, were those trees that were like 200 years old ones that survived the 1868 fire?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No, they were real young. They were about this size right here, something like that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: In 1868 they were, but when you logged it how old were they?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You’re talking about Weyerhaeuser here. Weyerhaeuser logged this after the Columbus Day windstorm in 1962. Everything you see here clear in the distance, it's all Weyerhaeuser.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But the Weyerhaeuser trees were 1750 to 1770 so, the hundred million feet your talking about, that was Weyerhaeuser timber?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, the hundred million, I just threw that figure out.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was a combination: state timber and Weyerhaeuser.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But were those the ones dated to 1750 or 1770?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, they would be.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Wow. That was a big tree.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That’s right. Here is where we enter the Elliott Forest. I'm not sure if it's called the Elliott Forest anymore but this is where you enter state property. Right around here. And the picture on the cover of my book was taken right here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So this is the first logging sale on the south end?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: 1958 this was sold, about fourteen million feet. This is called Eleven Creek down here to the left and that was . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That sale was called . . .

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: The Eleven Creek Headwaters?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think it was called Marlow Ridge, was what it was called.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: So that's how they cleared to the ridge top over there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So this on the left, is this regenerated since the sale?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yes, see after the 1958 timber sale . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So this would be 60 years old?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: seeded and this was back when we were so naive, it appeared all we had to do was harvest the old growth and you burn the slash and you aerial seed it with a helicopter, and you just stand back and watch it all grow up. It's so simple, we thought.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Because we were surrounded by a million acres of 70 year old timber, the south end of the Siuslaw and this, that it looks like you couldn't go wrong with those three things. Harvest, burn, aerial seed and you’re done.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Ten dollars an acre to do that. Then, oh . . . then we begin to realize it's not that simple. entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Did you have mountain beaver right here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay and then those small spindly trees that are growing up with the larger trees, would that be part of the aerial seeding? That they just haven't touched back into or would those be 60 year old stand with off-site seed maybe?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And then you were saying, a 170 years old, you were calling them old growth. Did you call them old growth in the 50's?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We did. Yeah. We just recognized. We had the 70 year old third growth and the next age class, which was 170 some.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Was that called mature second growth?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We all called it old growth because the loggers did. Loggers called it that. So we did too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Did you have any yellow fir up through here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No. No. This is only a handful of that on the whole forest. That stuff is 300 years old. The yellow fir.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh. Okay. Wow.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.text: And the logging operators, they knew BLM. They knew how BLM would react to it and the Forest Service. They didn't know anything about state and we weren't quite sure what to do either. entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I wonder, could there have been compaction that caused the off-site seed in the cat logging to . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I don't think we'll ever know that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.text: Now the big bank of alder over on the far hill over there. And maple. That's gotta be state land, too.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross

entries.speaker: Amber Ross

entries.text: Right in here?

entries.text: Right in here. They found a bird so that eliminated that timber.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.text: Well some bird.

entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Just a little bit in the background is a patch of older timber in there. That was one of those Indian allotments.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Oh.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: There were three of them in here. That was one of the Indian . . . Just to show how impractical those were when they signed those Dawes Act allotments. That's one.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We acquired it from a private owner that bought it from BIA [Bureau of Indian Affairs].

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I'm interested in finding out more about those allotments, because I'm just not familiar with any that got assigned in country like this. It seems like a special type of thing they must've done.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well I don’t even know nothing about it, virtually.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I know about the Dawes Act, but only in the Umatilla Reservation, and that; where they first started it. And then the coastal areas where they had reservations set up, but they didn't have a reservation here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No they didn't.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's what makes it kind of interesting.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: What I understood was that there was a decision not to create a reservation. That's after they failed to ratify the original one. And so then they just randomly almost assigned these 160s like that one. And the one that actually got lived on is down at Johnson Point. Well we call it Indian Point, but it's . . . and that did get lived on, even though there was really nowhere to live, it got used. It was on the creek. So we had a pretty good size land exchange where we acquired all three of these.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And how big were those, were they half sections?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Quarters.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Quarters.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: And by now I'll bet that. I bet it's full of birds now, too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I’m going to take two or three panoramas right here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. So one of the allotments is on top of that peak there?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, right there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Who's allotment was that? Any idea?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I don't know what the Indian family's name was. We know the middle one, Indian Point down there, was Johnson.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: All the allotments, when they first put the Dawes Act in, all the ones were reservations, and then the Indians got to choose, and the big deal was that the French Canadians were eligible for Donation Land Claims, for Homestead Act claims, and then also for Dawes Act claims, and so that's created real problems, political problems, right up through today. Mostly between families, not between governments.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well the only ones that I'm aware of here that had any real value are those that now are the elk pasture down by Reedsport. That was another one there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: At Dean's Creek there?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Mm-hmm (affirmative). That big pasture there.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: And there's a couple that border the highway, but they're basically rock outcrops.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Allotments? Wow.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's one of the many things I learned today. I had no idea. Jerry, I think I asked earlier, but I'm not sure we got it recorded right, but there's a lot of landslides in this country and you were saying that the roads exacerbated that.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Mainly the roads. We pushed a side cast over the edge, and that has caused a few slides.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You ever see any difference between clearcuts, non-clearcuts, and unlogged areas?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I'd say, this is what I've just observed, yeah, I'd say there's a few more in the harvest areas.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Do those usually occur within a few years of harvest?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, they do.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. And could that have been like the method of harvest? Could you go into those areas and say you log by helicopter, instead of high lead and reduce potential for landside?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Oh yeah. I think so.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So it's caused more by roughing up the ground than by removing the trees?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, there's been studies on that. And I shouldn't pretend to really know anything as far as on the ground. After whichever time that was . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah, I think '61, and then '82 was years when there were a lot of landslides.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Maybe '82 there was quite a bit of on the ground surveys in those places. And I never even read a final report of that. They said, "Well there was some question on that," but I would certainly believe that there's some more on the harvest areas. The clearcut areas. They say well, once the vegetation is dead it's root holding capacity decreases. It makes sense to me.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: And there seems to be almost always when you see a large clearcut area, and by large I mean let's say more than 20 acres, you do see almost always some small land movements. Now those that are in a ravine are properly called “debris avalanches.” Because there may be no actual lands moved, but there's a lot of debris that has moved in the water course. (silence)

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's another thing, on steep land where it worked in the past, there's a lot of pistol-butted trees because the soils just keep moving.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I'm guessing that you got the same situation here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think so. I can't say any particular place, but individual trees, yeah. Let me see here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That patch of old-growth back there, is that part of the Mill Creek watershed old-growth that you're talking about?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, it is.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. Just a little patch of them.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well we successfully acquired all the private land of this whole ridge. There's still little pieces of BLM at the bottom. But what happened was that many years ago, I mean 45 years ago, something like that, the State Department of Forestry through a lot of effort -- one man spent a whole year working out a land exchange with the BLM, and a BLM man did too, and when they got clear through the whole process, BLM declared, well they weren't going to do it because they put a change in their age classes.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: At that point, the State Forestry Department says okay, that's it. Never another one. They wasted all that man-hours of time for nothing.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: You were managing this on an age class of 100 years, then it became 90 years . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right. 90.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And then in '62, all the 70-year-old trees blew over. What happens to an age class when nature strikes?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You deal with it. We harvested 300 million feet, all in one clout.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. After that point, did you try to go back to an age class rotation again?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No, we just ignored it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh good. Did you just start doing it on volume and acreage at that point?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: You know that was the interesting thing, because we were running on an acreage control with the volume in check. That's what it was declared to be. 500 acres of clearcut a year with a volume of, and of course the volume is going to vary . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And in your book, you said the line of demarcation in the management of the forest was before and after the Columbus Day storm, but then it seems to me like another mark might be the spotted owl in 1990, that everything changed at that point as well.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It did. Although it seems to me that the marbled murrelet has a bigger impact with the owl. That to me was an example of the . . . It's a bad story along that line. There was a declaration by, I don't know who it was, Fish and Wildlife, or that may be who it was, in Oregon, there should be 1000 pairs, breeding pairs, of spotted owls. And they said okay, so BLM said they would take 400 pairs and be responsible for those, Forest Service says they would take 400 pairs, be responsible for those, and they said you on the Elliott Forest will be responsible for four pairs.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We said, "Good, we know right where they are. Right in this canyon right here. We almost have names for them, we know them so well. These four pairs in here. Good." And later they said, "Well actually you have more than four. And they are in older trees than 70," or whatever the figure was. Clearly they don't have to have old-growth. They said, "But all these other

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: owls that you have are unhappy owls because they're being forced to live in trees that are not old-growth. They moved from the Weyerhaeuser tree farm over to you. But you got to sympathize, they're not happy owls." Okay.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I hope they didn't put that in print.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: And then that of course I have to remind you immediately of the fact that we spent millions of dollars taking anything that resembled wood out of the creeks. Now we're spending a lot of money putting wood back into the creeks. Just because some biologist says something, doesn't mean a tick in the long run. And they don't ever say they're sorry.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well that's what's curious about some of that, because the fish biologists here 50 years ago were not only cleaning the creeks, they were blasting away rock to get rid of the waterfalls and things. Or at least recommending it. So that's a 180 in how they manage. And the same with the forest pretty much.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Are we looking for Indian Point?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah. It's coming up.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.text: Okay. That's just right after Indian Point, isn't it?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's a little bit more.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Isn't it at the confluence? The Umpqua?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: What's that?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Isn't it at the mouth?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It is.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But they had to build some kind of impoundment for the . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well you know that to me is a curious thing. If it was a water powered mill, which seems like it must have been, there is no actual cascade of running water down the hillside to use.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Could they have used the tide? That wouldn't be enough power, would it?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It doesn't seem like it.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I wonder if it was just one of those hand tidewaters like they have in the South. Two guys and a whipsaw.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: As far as I know, nobody knows.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well they built a couple ships.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: They did. Now I got all that out of [Jerry] Winterbotham’s book [Umpqua – The Lost County of Oregon, 1994].

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: So we are surrounded by state land right now.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I even went to visit him over in Brownsville. I went over to ask him permission to use that story out of his book in my book. He was a schoolteacher at Elkton. That's what he had been. Jerry Winterbotham.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: I wonder if the GLO notes have anything on that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Coastal Geodetic Surveys.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, Coast Geodetic. That's what it was. I wonder if they'd have anything?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: walked down, there was a trail, I walked right down here, and that's where the Johnson family lived. Right on the edge of the water down there.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was just a little bitty quarter acre of land that you could live on, and I guess they did. I tried one time to go and . . . The Johnsons are still living, but she's living up at Siletz.” And she says, "Well I'm going to talk to her." “Okay.” That's the only one that we know of that they lived on in this canyon here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Now if they lived right there, I'm going to take a picture or two right here, but if the allotment was right down here next to the water . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Down to the right.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So they ran logs from up here.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's back here a ways.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh okay, so a canoe would be no problem then.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I guess. Yeah. Of all the things that happened historically, because today it would be unthinkable.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Yeah. What is Indian Point exactly? Is it just the point of land that goes down up in here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's starts right here. It's a little steep, a peninsula, that runs right down here to the creek.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We sold our timber sale here. It was all the way across the creek, and all the hillside there. And they brought in a yarder that sat on this side, and they used a skyline to bring all that wood across, above the water over, to this side to chuck it out. But we did it.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: That's pretty impressive, all the different methods they've come up with.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It is. Loggers historically have been very creative. And those all had a name to them, all the different systems.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Well that's nice to know that that road leads right down to the . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It does.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: It does. I walked down it. There wasn't any structures left that we saw. But you can see kind of a flat area where they probably would've had a house. Some of the brush was pretty thick.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What's that?

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Some of the brush was pretty thick.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's why I like the old surveys and vegetation patterns and then you get the aerial photo, so you can really start to . . .

entries.speaker: Amber Ross

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yeah, I took points at all the stops we made today.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh wonderful.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: So I can . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So I didn't need a USGS map at all.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: And I can print you the map when we're done.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Yes.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Now, right in here. Here for the next few hundred feet is flat ground. That is where the buildings and the mill had to be. There's no one spot. If you went another few hundred feet here on the right-hand side, there used to be a big crabapple tree. I don't know if it's still there or not. The trees that are here now are all the ones that we planted.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So that's a plantation out there?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It's a plantation.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. What is that about 40?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It was a big blackberry patch, and we turned a blackberry patch into a plantation. We acquired all the private land in the whole canyon here, and we did it because we wanted to be responsible for the whole thing. Instead of being blamed if someone did something.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Do you think in retrospect was that a good move?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think it was. We tried to maintain good public relations with our neighbors.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: There's lots of flat area over there, too.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, on the other side. Oh yeah.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: They thought that was the main camp.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, and look at the right down there. It looks like there's an incline coming down just on the other side of the blackberries.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: We built, all above your heads, all the roads. There's a switchback. And it goes clear to the top of the ridge.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: There's an old roadway on the other side there.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, that's what it is. That's the haul road.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Oh, okay.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: It might be gated. I'm not positive on that.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Is that BLM over there?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: No, it's Elliott Forest. See we acquired all the private land here.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Except for this little chunk straight in front of us is private.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: To the left, there is a little teeny strip of BLM.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Ah, this is BLM land. We are right on time.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Perfect.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: And there's also some pilings under this bridge.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Old ones? Well, it seems like since they were running ships and things that that would be a docking place, a pretty logical one.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Jerry thought it might've been part of the old mill.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: The thing back here that always blows my mind is in my source book there. It says this guy who was occupying those grounds has a mill there, and a ship building yard. They were down in San Francisco, and they didn't like the whole country down there, so they looked for a better place than all that country, and they stayed at the Umpqua and chose this. That's kind of hard to believe. There's a whole shipbuilding yard built out there. There's no place that looked good to them, so they came up here.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: We're going to go by Luder Creek and Charlotte.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: That's right.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: And you thought that Charlotte Creek had some kind of association with Indians as well?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well I think it did and probably . . . I'm not sure about Luder Creek. Luder Creeks is kind of a canyon.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That sounds more like a German guy.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: But I think Charlotte Creek and Indian Charlie Creek both those probably had Indians.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: What's the reason you think that?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Well, Indian Charlie Creek, I think, because when I came to work here, that's 65 years ago, so that's a long time, but local people said that there was an Indian cemetery up there on Indian Charlie Creek, but a gyppo logger moved up in there in 1951, and had private land there that had a landing, that probably wrecked whatever there was of an Indian cemetery if there ever was one there.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Hmm. First couple of miles?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: And Charlotte Creek, because there's quite a little bit of flat land right there.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Luder Creek, does it have any tidal action? I've only stopped by there a couple of times, and it's been pretty dry.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I kind of doubt that it does . . .

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Okay. It looks just like almost a seasonal drainage.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: See all this on the right-hand side would've been part of that Charlotte Creek. It was an Indian allotment or whatever it was.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: On the right here?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I'm just saying this would've connected with the . . . the claim would've been in the mouth of the Charlotte Creek on the left.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: So that whole flat right through there, that's all natural?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah, it is.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: Wow. Oh, I see what you're saying.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: I think the Charlotte Creek would've been a land claim right here so . . . It probably has an Indian background.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: It would seem like it. It sure looks like the topography would sure fit.

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Yeah.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: That's why I was curious about the name. There's still a lot of Johnsons in the Siletz area. Would that be the same family?

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: It sure might be. It's a very common North American name. More commonly used than Smith.

entries.speaker: Amber Ross
entries.text: Oh, wow.

entries.speaker: Bob Zybach
entries.text: But to have an Indian named Johnson is less common. And then to have a relative with the same name would be . . . But that Charlotte Creek area there, that looks like it really could've been a village site or at least a . . .

entries.speaker: Jerry Phillips
entries.text: Sure does to me. What Indians seem to do, and African Americans, too, they just adopt a name that they kind of liked that was available. My kinfolks came to Maryland in 1660 or something like that, and they had 12 black slaves on their property list when they died, and those folks got their freedom in Maryland when they turned age 31. So they just adopted the name of the family they were living with and carried on.
